section.title: Israel Has Not Returned
section.sectionRationale: Amos indicts the pampered women of Samaria, mocks the busy false worship at Bethel and Gilgal, and then recites a series of escalating disasters God has already sent, each punctuated by the same heartbreaking refrain: yet you did not return to Me. The chapter ends with a summons to prepare to meet God and a soaring hymn to His majesty.
section.thesis: God had sent famine, drought, blight, plague, and defeat as merciful warnings meant to turn Israel back, but they would not return; so now they must brace to meet the Maker of the mountains face to face.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the cows of Bashan and the beloved false worship; the fivefold refrain of disasters that failed to turn Israel back; and the summons to meet God, sealed with a hymn to the Creator.

units.label: The cows of Bashan and the worship they love
units.note: luxury on the backs of the poor

verses.text: Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, you women who oppress the poor and crush the needy, who say to your husbands, “Bring us more to drink.”
The Lord GOD has sworn by His holiness: “Behold, the days are coming when you will be taken away with hooks, and your posterity with fishhooks.
You will go out through broken walls, each one straight ahead of her, and you will be cast out toward Harmon,” declares the LORD.
“Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal! Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days.
Offer leavened bread as a thank offering, and loudly proclaim your freewill offerings. For that is what you children of Israel love to do,” declares the Lord GOD.
“I afflicted all your cities with cleanness of teeth and all your towns with lack of bread, yet you did not {{shuv|return}} to Me,” declares the LORD.
“I also withheld the rain from you when the harvest was three months away. I sent rain on one city but withheld it from another. One field received rain; another without rain withered.
People staggered from city to city for water to drink, but they were not satisfied; yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
“I struck you with blight and mildew in your growing gardens and vineyards; the locust devoured your fig and olive trees, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.

“I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt; I killed your young men with the sword, along with your captured horses. I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
“Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD.
“Therefore, that is what I will do to you, O Israel, and since I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel!

For behold, He who forms the mountains, who creates the wind and reveals His thoughts to man, who turns the dawn to darkness and strides on the heights of the earth, the LORD, the God of {{tsevaot|Hosts}}, is His name.”

shuv.gloss: To turn, turn back, return; the ordinary Hebrew word for repentance, picturing a person walking away from God who turns around and comes home. The refrain yet you did not return to Me tolls five times in this chapter, revealing that all God's disciplines were designed to bring Israel back, and that the tragedy is not the disasters but the refusal to turn.

tsevaot.gloss: Hosts, armies; the title LORD of Hosts pictures God as commander of all the armies of heaven and the powers of creation. The chapter's closing hymn crowns the summons to meet God: the One Israel must face is the Maker of mountains and wind, the God of Hosts, whose very name declares that no creature can stand against Him.

basic.context: Amos rebukes the wealthy women of Samaria, calling them fat cows of Bashan who press their husbands for more luxury paid for by crushing the poor. He then mocks their eager, showy worship at Bethel and Gilgal, which they love but which God hates. Next he lists disasters God had already sent, famine, drought, crop failure, plague, defeat, each ending with the refrain, yet you did not return to Me. Because every warning failed, Israel must now prepare to meet God Himself.
basic.hermeneutics: The disasters were not blind bad luck; they were God's merciful alarm bells, sent to turn Israel back before it was too late. The chapter shows that judgment is often God's severe mercy, and that the real tragedy is a heart that will not repent even under discipline. Prepare to meet your God is both a threat and, implicitly, a last call.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain turns on shuv, to return or repent, picturing someone turning around and coming home; five times God says you did not shuv to Me. The chapter ends by naming God the LORD of Hosts, tsevaot, commander of heaven's armies and all creation, the One they must face.
basic.typology: The God who disciplines in order to bring His people back foreshadows the Father who disciplines those He loves, and the summons prepare to meet your God points to the final meeting every person will have with God, a meeting made safe only in Christ.
basic.christ: Israel could not, and would not, return to God on their own; the failure of every warning exposes the need for a Savior who turns the heart. Jesus is the one in whom we can prepare to meet God without terror, for He met the judgment we deserved. The showy worship God rejected finds its answer in worship in spirit and truth, made possible through Christ.
basic.god: God is patient and merciful, sending warning after warning before final judgment. He is grieved, not gleeful, over an unrepentant people. And He is the almighty Creator, the God of Hosts, whom no one can resist and everyone must eventually meet.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 12 shows God disciplining those He loves as sons. Romans 2 warns against presuming on God's patience. Revelation 6 pictures the terror of facing God apart from Christ.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows a God who wounds in order to heal and warns in order to save, and a people who will not turn. It deepens the ache for the One who can finally turn hearts home and make the meeting with God a homecoming rather than a horror.

context.literary:
Amos 4 is the second of the 'Hear this word' sermons, and it has the neatest shape in the book. It moves in four stages. Verses 1 to 3 are a woe-like address to the wealthy women of Samaria, with a sentence introduced by an oath. Verses 4 and 5 are a bitter parody of a priest's call to worship. Verses 6 to 11 are the great refrain, five paragraphs of disaster each ending 'yet you did not return to Me.' Verses 12 and 13 are the climax: a summons, and a hymn.

The parody of verses 4 and 5 is worth seeing in its shape. A priest at a shrine might call out, 'Come to Bethel and worship.' Amos uses the same tone and changes one word: 'Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal.' The commands that follow are ordinary acts of piety, sacrifice in the morning, tithes, thank offerings and freewill offerings, but they are heaped up with an increasing sarcasm until the last line, 'For that is what you children of Israel love to do.' The line is a stab at the true object of their love. They love the ritual; they do not love the God it was meant for.

The refrain of verses 6 to 11 is built like a lament. Each disaster is described in a verse or two, in the first person, 'I afflicted,' 'I withheld,' 'I struck,' 'I sent,' 'I overthrew,' and each ends with the same sentence. The disasters escalate, from hunger to drought to blight and locust to plague and war and finally to something like Sodom. The refrain then breaks off. The reader expects a sixth stroke, and instead the speaker says, 'Therefore, that is what I will do to you,' without saying what it is. The unnamed 'this' is the sentence for which the refrain has been preparing, and the silence makes it heavier than any named punishment.

The final verse, the first of three hymns in the book, 4:13, 5:8-9 and 9:5-6, answers the missing sentence with a portrait of the one who will do it. The hymn is a string of participles in praise of God as maker and ruler, and each of its clauses is a reason to take the summons of verse 12 seriously.
context.historical:
Bashan is the fertile highland east of the Jordan, known in Israel for its cattle and its rams, Deuteronomy 32:14 and Psalm 22:12, and the cows of Bashan are therefore the best-fed animals the audience could picture. The women addressed are presumably the wives of the Samaritan elite, whose luxury is financed by the people they 'oppress.' Their demand to their 'lords,' 'Bring us more to drink,' shows that the pursuit of pleasure is the engine behind the exploitation.

The sentence of verses 2 and 3 describes the sort of deportation that Assyria would later practise. Captives were led away with ropes or rings attached to their noses or lips, and the Old Testament uses the same image of hooks in the nose for the humiliation of conquered peoples, Isaiah 37:29 and Ezekiel 29:4. The 'broken walls,' each woman walking straight ahead through a breach, is a picture of a captured city, and Harmon, which the footnote suggests may be Mount Hermon, points north toward the road to exile.

Bethel and Gilgal were the great shrines of the northern kingdom, and Amos returns to them in 5:4-5 with the instruction not to seek them. Gilgal was the place of Israel's first camp in the land, Joshua 4:19, which gave it a rich history. The tithe 'every three days' appears in some translations as 'every three years,' as the BSB footnote notes, and the law did prescribe a tithe for the poor every third year, Deuteronomy 14:28-29. Whichever reading is followed, the point is zeal at the shrine, outrunning what was required.

The disasters are the ones that the covenant itself had named. Leviticus 26:14-26 and Deuteronomy 28:15-68 spell out famine, drought, crop failure, pestilence, defeat in war and overthrow as the consequences of covenant breach, and Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, 1 Kings 8:33-40, imagines every one of them and asks that God would forgive if His people turned back. Haggai, a long time afterward, uses the same words, 'blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me,' Haggai 2:17. Amos is therefore not announcing something new. He is telling Israel that the sequence the law had warned of has already happened, and the repentance the law had asked for has not.
context.canonical:
The refrain of chapter 4 is the Bible's most compact portrait of a people who will not turn. The call to return runs through the Prophets: Hosea 6:1, 'Come, let us return to the LORD'; Joel 2:12-13, 'return to Me with all your heart'; Malachi 3:7, 'Return to Me, and I will return to you.' Amos 4 is the counterpart, the record of the invitation that went unanswered. Isaiah 9:13 puts it in the same terms: the people did not turn to Him who struck them. Jeremiah 5:3 says they refused to repent.

The discipline of chapter 4 is taken up in the New Testament in two directions. Hebrews 12:5-11 reads God's discipline of His people as the work of a father who disciplines a son he loves, 'for our good, so that we may share in His holiness.' Revelation 3:19 says, 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent.' At the same time Revelation shows the failure of discipline: in the plagues of Revelation 9:20-21 and Revelation 16:9, people who are struck 'did not repent.' The refrain of Amos is clearly in the ear of the seer of Patmos.

The 'brand snatched from a blaze,' verse 11, is the picture used of Joshua the high priest in Zechariah 3:2, who is cleansed and given clean clothes, and Jude 23 says of the believers to be rescued, 'save others by snatching them from the fire.' Paul's remark, 'God's kindness leads you to repentance,' Romans 2:4, gives the hope that lay under every disaster in Amos 4.

The summons 'Prepare to meet your God' echoes Exodus 19:11-17, where the people are told to be ready for the third day and Moses brings them out to meet God. The language is the language of Sinai. Finally the hymn of verse 13 has companions in Amos 5:8-9 and 9:5-6, in Job 9:5-10 and in Psalm 104, and it is picked up in the New Testament in Jesus' mastery over the wind, Mark 4:39-41.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos meant the hearers to recognise their own recent history. Everything in verses 6 to 11 was something that had happened or could have been remembered: a hungry year, a drought in the weeks before harvest, a blighted vineyard, a locust swarm, a war with its dead horses and unburied bodies, a town overturned. In each case the hearers had explained it by some other cause. Amos says that the LORD sent these things and that each was a call to return. By repeating the same line five times, he means to make it impossible to hear the list as a series of accidents.

He also meant to reveal what their religion had become. The call to worship in verses 4 and 5 shows that all the energy of their devotion is directed to a ritual that God has not asked for and is not receiving. The eagerness of the worshippers is one of the things being judged. Amos is not complaining that they have stopped coming to the shrine; he is complaining that they come and are unchanged.

And he meant to leave the hearers with a task and not just a threat. 'Prepare to meet your God' is a command, and it assumes that preparation is possible. The great hymn that follows is not there to frighten them into silence but to make clear who it is they are to meet. It would have been natural to read the whole chapter as a final judgment with no way back. The imperative, and the very existence of the refrain, say that the way back was still open for those who would take it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes particular events and a particular sentence. It does not teach that every famine or crop failure is a punishment for the sins of the people who suffer it. The covenant relationship between God and Israel was unique, and the book of Job and the words of Jesus about the Galileans killed by Pilate, Luke 13:1-5, both reject the easy inference from suffering to sin. The passage does show that God can use hardship to call people back, and that one of the things hardship is for is to ask the question 'Will you return?'

What it prescribes by implication is the response. When God's discipline comes, in any form, the right reaction is to turn to Him and not to harden. That applies to the church as much as to Israel. Hebrews 12 encourages believers not to lose heart when they are disciplined. It also prescribes a way of examining worship: God asks whether our devotions are matched by changed lives. The mocking invitation to Bethel is a warning to every congregation whose zeal for ritual outruns its love for the people God loves. And the closing summons applies to everyone: to be ready to meet God is not a threat to be postponed but a standing responsibility.

debates.question: Who are the 'cows of Bashan,' and who are their 'husbands'?

views.label: The wives of the wealthy of Samaria
views.case: The address is feminine, and the Hebrew word translated 'husbands' means literally 'their lords.' On this reading Amos is speaking to the women of the elite, who press their men for more luxury while the poor are crushed. The image of a well-fed herd matches the picture of comfortable women.

views.label: The ruling class as a whole
views.case: Others take the feminine form as a figure of speech for the whole upper class, in the way a prophet might use a feminine noun for a city or nation. Amos 6:1 addresses the leaders of Samaria in the masculine, and the two charges may be two ways of speaking to the same class.

views.label: A deliberately shocking insult
views.case: A third emphasis holds that the point is the insult itself. Cattle are being fattened for slaughter, and the language of fishhooks in verse 2 completes the picture of animals led off to be butchered. The identity of the speakers matters less than the image.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the people addressed are those who profit from the poor and who think their ease is secure. The identity of the women does not change the application: no one is exempt because they did not personally commit the injustice, if they demand its fruits.

debates.question: Is the call to worship in verses 4 and 5 sarcasm, or a literal permission?

views.label: Irony
views.case: The invitation to 'transgress' at the shrine is an inversion of the normal priestly call. Amos is not telling the people to rebel. He is saying that their worship is rebellion. The final sentence, 'that is what you love to do,' supports this, since God never says that He loves what they do.

views.label: A claim about specific irregularities
views.case: Some commentators have noted that the offering of leavened bread as a thank offering is in tension with Leviticus 2:11, which forbids burning leaven on the altar, though Leviticus 7:12-13 allows leavened loaves to be presented with the thanksgiving offering. They suggest that Amos is pointing at actual departures from the law, such as offering what was only to be presented. The text does not make this clear.

debates.bearing: The two readings do not exclude each other. The central charge is not about ritual details but about worship that has no connection to justice, as Isaiah 1:11-17 says. The details of the offerings are secondary.

debates.question: Is 'Prepare to meet your God' a threat or an invitation?

views.label: A threat
views.case: The 'therefore' that begins verse 12 ties the summons to the failure of every warning. The scene is Sinai, where the people were told to prepare and the mountain shook, Exodus 19:11-17. On this reading the summons is the last word of a judge: God is coming, and there is nothing left to say.

views.label: A final call to repentance
views.case: The imperative assumes that preparation is possible and that it matters. Amos 5:4, 'Seek Me and live,' shows that the door was still open. On this reading the line is a last summons to do what the refrain says Israel had refused to do.

debates.bearing: The two readings are probably one. The line is a threat to those who will not respond and an invitation to those who will. This double edge is characteristic of the prophets, who warn so that the warning may do its work.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the pun in the opening address. The women are 'cows of Bashan,' parot, and they speak to their 'lords,' adoneihem, the plural of adon, the word for master. The Hebrew is plain about the relationships: the women who order their masters about are themselves the masters of the poor, whom they 'oppress' and 'crush.' Both verbs are strong ones, for violent pressure and breaking in pieces. The scene is a house where the top commands the bottom down the line, and the demand at the bottom of the chain, 'Bring us more to drink,' is the final result.

The oath of verse 2 is unusual: the Lord GOD 'has sworn by His holiness.' Elsewhere in Amos He swears by Himself, 6:8, and by 'the pride of Jacob,' 8:7. To swear by His holiness is to put the whole of His character behind the sentence. Hebrews 6:13 says that God swore by Himself because there was no one greater, and the oath of Amos is the same kind of act.

The phrase 'cleanness of teeth,' verse 6, is an idiom for hunger. The footnote explains it as 'empty stomachs.' It is a grimly vivid phrase, with teeth that have nothing to dirty them. The pair 'blight and mildew' in verse 9, shiddafon and yeraqon, is a stock pair that occurs in the covenant curses, Deuteronomy 28:22, in Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:37, and in Haggai 2:17. Hearers would have recognised the formula from the law.

The verb for the Sodom overthrow in verse 11 is the one used in Genesis 19:25 for what God did to the cities, hafakh, to turn over, overturn. The footnote on the 'firebrand' in the same verse says 'a burning stick,' which is the sense of the Hebrew, a piece of wood pulled out of the fire before it is consumed. It describes a rescue that was only just in time. Zechariah 3:2 uses the same figure for Joshua the high priest.

In verse 12, 'prepare' is the verb kun, to set firm or make ready, and 'meet' is the ordinary word for going out to meet someone. Together the clause speaks of someone setting himself in order for an encounter that is about to take place. In Exodus 19:11-17, where the people are to be ready for the third day and then Moses brings them out 'to meet with God,' the vocabulary is close, and the hearers of Amos would have recognised the allusion to Sinai.

The unspecified 'this' of verse 12 is also worth noticing. The Hebrew says, 'So I will do to you, Israel; and because I will do this to you, prepare.' The thing to be done is never named, and the reader is left to supply it. The refusal to specify is a rhetorical device that makes the threat larger.

The hymn of verse 13 is a string of participles, so that God is described by what He is always doing: forming, creating, declaring, making, treading. 'Forms' is the verb used of the potter, yatsar, as in Genesis 2:7. 'Treads' is the verb used of a conqueror marching over a land. The 'high places' of the earth are the bamot, which in Israel's idiom were also the hills where altars stood. God walks on the very summits where the Israelites worshipped what was not God. The word for 'wind' is ruach, which can also mean breath or spirit, and the verse speaks of making it as readily as of forming mountains. The phrase translated 'reveals His thoughts to man' is difficult in the Hebrew, since the pronoun could refer to the man, and some translators render it 'declares to man what is his thought.' The BSB takes it as God's thoughts, which suits the context of a God who has been speaking to Israel through disasters and through the prophet.

typology.type: The brand snatched from the fire, Amos 4:11
typology.fulfillment: Israel is a charred stick pulled out of the blaze, saved at the last moment. Zechariah applies the same picture to Joshua the high priest, who stands in filthy clothes and is cleansed, Zechariah 3:2-4. The correspondence is of a rescue that is entirely God's. In the New Testament believers are called to snatch others from the fire, Jude 23, and Christ is the one who has rescued His people from the coming wrath, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. The escalation is that the rescue is not a late escape from disaster but a full cleansing, with the filthy garments exchanged for clean ones. The type falls short because the brand is still scorched, while Christ makes new creatures, 2 Corinthians 5:17.

The disasters are the discipline of a God who wants His people back. Hebrews 12:5-11 reads discipline as the training of a son, 'for our good, so that we may share in His holiness,' and Revelation 3:19 puts it in the voice of Christ: 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline.' The correspondence is that discipline is a sign of love. The escalation is that Jesus Himself learned obedience through what He suffered, Hebrews 5:8, and so shares the pattern from the inside. The type falls short because Israel's failure to turn shows that discipline alone does not change hearts.

The summons draws on Sinai, where the people were to be ready for a meeting that shook the mountain. In the New Testament the forerunner is John, who goes before the Lord to 'make ready a people prepared for the Lord,' Luke 1:17, and the voice in the wilderness cries, 'Prepare the way for the Lord,' Matthew 3:3. The correspondence is of a God who comes and a people who must be ready. The escalation is that the One who comes is Jesus, Immanuel, and those who are in Him can face the meeting with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. The type falls short in that Sinai kept the people at a distance, while Christ brings them near.

typology.type: The Maker of the wind, Amos 4:13
typology.fulfillment: The hymn names God as the one who creates the wind and walks the heights. When Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea and they obey Him, His disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:39-41. The correspondence is of the same authority over the same elements. The escalation is that Colossians 1:16 says all things were created through Him and for Him. This is not a hidden prophecy of Jesus in Amos 4:13. It is a way in which the New Testament identifies the person who walks among the disciples with the one the hymn praises.

study.christ:
The chapter does not mention a rescuer, and its mood is one of the bleakest in the book. It leads to Christ chiefly by showing what the failure to return looks like and what kind of intervention would be needed.

The first link is the problem. Five times God says that He has done everything short of the last thing, and five times the people did not return. Hosea says the same thing in other words, 'Come, let us return to the LORD,' Hosea 6:1, and then complains that the people's love is like a morning mist, Hosea 6:4. If a nation could not be turned by famine, drought, blight, locust, plague, war and a catastrophe like Sodom, then no amount of external pressure would turn it. The need is not for harsher discipline but for a different kind of heart. That is what the new covenant promises, 'I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you,' Ezekiel 36:26, and what the New Testament says Christ does, 2 Corinthians 5:17. The weight of Amos 4 is a long pointer to a salvation that has to change people from inside.

The second link is the God who comes. 'Prepare to meet your God' is the summons of Sinai, and the gospel proclaims that the God who was met on the mountain has come among people in Jesus. John the Baptist is sent to prepare the way, Luke 1:17, and the child who is born is called Immanuel, God with us, Matthew 1:23. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and says that the city did not recognise 'the time of your visitation from God,' Luke 19:41-44. The meeting that Amos announced as a sentence has taken place in a person, and He has come to rescue and not only to judge. Those who prepare by receiving Him can meet God without terror, for 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1.

The third link is the brand plucked from the fire. The verse is about Israel's near destruction, but the New Testament takes the image into the picture of those saved from the fire of judgment. Jude 23 asks believers to snatch others from the fire, and the first Christians knew that they themselves had been snatched, 1 Thessalonians 1:10. In Zechariah's vision, the brand is Joshua, whose dirty garments are removed, and the removal of the garments is a picture of forgiveness, Zechariah 3:4. The clean garments of that vision are what Christ gives to His people.

The fourth link is worship. The sacrifices of verses 4 and 5 are numerous and loud and unaccepted. The letter to the Hebrews declares that the repeated sacrifices of the old order could never make worshippers perfect, Hebrews 10:1-4, and that Christ has offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, Hebrews 10:12. Jesus Himself says that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, John 4:23-24. What Israel tried to buy with offerings is given freely in the one offering of the Son.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The cows, the hooks and the locusts are not hidden portraits of Christ. The chapter points to Him by raising the problem to which He is the answer and by the way its images are taken up in the New Testament.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the speaker of every disaster. 'I afflicted,' 'I withheld,' 'I struck,' 'I sent,' 'I overthrew.' The first-person verbs are meant to be heard one after the other, and they make the claim that these were no accidents of weather and war. The Bible's wider teaching on God's rule over rain, harvest and nations, Deuteronomy 11:13-17 and Matthew 5:45, stands behind this. The doctrine is hard, and the passage does not try to soften it. It does show, however, that these acts have a purpose, and that the purpose is stated in the refrain: that they would return.

That makes the main thing the chapter shows about God His patience. A judge who only wanted to punish would not have sent warnings at graded intervals. The disasters begin with the lighter and rise to the heavier. In the selective rains of verse 7, one city is watered while another goes dry, so the severity is measured and the pain is pointed. A God who aimed only at destruction would not have been so careful. Paul's question in Romans 2:4 has the right tone: 'Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads you to repentance?'

God is a Father who cares about the response. The failure of the people to return is described as the thing that matters most. The sentence is not 'you suffered' but 'you did not return to Me.' The phrase 'to Me' is the heart of it. The destination is not a better harvest or a safer border but a restored relationship. In the fullest picture of God's heart in Hosea 11:8, He asks, 'How can I give you up, O Ephraim?' and Amos 4 records the point at which the answer begins to be 'I must.'

He is a holy God who cannot be bought. The offerings at Bethel and Gilgal are lavish, and He is not interested. The same truth is in Isaiah 29:13, where the people honour Him with lips while their hearts are far away. He takes no delight in worship that does not come with a heart, and He does not hide His feeling. It is a kind of mercy that He says so.

He is the Creator who has no rival. The hymn of verse 13 draws on the language of forming and making, the shaping of mountains, the creation of wind, the turning of dawn into darkness, the treading of the heights. These are not decoration. The power that formed the world is the power that sent the disasters and is about to meet Israel. And His name is the LORD, the God of Hosts. The point is that there is no corner of the world where He is not.

For worship, the chapter asks the reader to read their own hardships with a question, 'What is God asking of me here?' and to answer by turning to Him and not by hardening. It asks too that worship be tested by its fruit. And it leaves us with a God who is as good as His word in the sentence and as good as His word in His offers of mercy: 'Return to Me, and I will return to you,' Malachi 3:7.

crossReferences.note: The covenant curses begin with terror and disease, then the sky like iron, then sword, plague and a cut supply of bread. More than once God says that if they will not accept discipline He will multiply the strokes. Amos 4:6-11 reads like a report of that chapter in action, with the same sequence and the same pedagogy of escalating discipline.

Among the curses for disobedience is a pair of crop diseases, blight and mildew, which are the same words that Amos 4:9 uses. The reader is expected to recognise the covenant language. What Moses said would follow disobedience, Amos says has already happened.

Solomon prays at the dedication of the temple about every sort of disaster, defeat, drought, famine, plague, blight, mildew and locusts, and asks God to hear and forgive when the people turn back. Amos shows each of those conditions as having been met, while the condition of turning has not been.

Haggai uses the language of Amos 4:9 in nearly the same words: God struck the work of their hands with blight, mildew and hail, but they did not turn to Him. The echo across two centuries shows that the pattern was well known and that the failure of Israel's repentance did not end with Amos.

Hosea gives the voice of the repentance that Amos says was missing, 'Come, let us return to the LORD,' and in the same breath exposes its shallowness: their love is like the morning mist. The two prophets, speaking to the same kingdom, together show a people who say the words but do not turn.

The LORD calls for return with all the heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning, and tells them to tear their hearts and not their garments, because He is gracious and compassionate and relents from sending disaster. It is the invitation Amos 4:6-11 shows being refused, with the character of the God to whom they could have returned.

Joshua the high priest stands in filthy clothes before the angel of the LORD, and the LORD says that he is a firebrand snatched from the fire. His clothes are removed and he is clothed with fine garments. This is the fullest development of the image used in Amos 4:11, and it adds the idea of cleansing.

The people are to be consecrated, wash their garments and be ready for the third day, and then Moses brings them out to meet with God. The call of Amos 4:12 to prepare to meet your God draws on this scene and makes clear that Israel is being summoned to a second Sinai, with the difference that now they are the ones in the dock.

The writer quotes Proverbs about the Lord who disciplines the son He loves and explains that discipline is painful at the time but yields a harvest of righteousness and peace. This is the New Testament's reading of the kind of hardships in Amos 4, applied to believers who are meant to respond with trust.

In the plagues of the last days, people are scorched with great heat and curse the name of God, yet they do not repent and give Him glory. The pattern of Amos 4, in which affliction is met with hardened hearts, is seen again at the end of the age. The refusal to return is a standing human problem.

study.oneStory:
The chapter belongs to the stretch of the Bible's story in which God, having rescued a people and given them a land, tries by every means to keep them. The covenant at Sinai had set out the terms. Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 gave the blessings for obedience and the curses for disobedience, and both chapters end with a promise: even in exile, if the people return, God will remember His covenant, Leviticus 26:40-45 and Deuteronomy 30:1-10. Amos 4 is the middle of that story, the point at which the curses have been felt and the return has not come.

The question that the chapter leaves open is the biggest one in the Old Testament: can a people return? The answer of the history is no. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria within a few decades of Amos, 2 Kings 17:5-23, and the writer of Kings explains that they would not listen and did not turn. Judah follows into Babylon. Even the people who returned from exile found that the old problems did not go away, as Haggai 2:17 and Malachi 3:7 make clear.

Yet the promise of return does not die. The prophets begin to speak of a day when God Himself will do the turning. 'Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, that we may return,' prays the writer of Lamentations 5:21. Jeremiah promises a new covenant in which the law is written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:31-34, and Ezekiel promises a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. These promises answer the refrain of Amos 4 directly. If the people cannot return, God will bring them back.

That is what the gospel announces. Jesus begins His ministry by saying, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near,' Matthew 4:17, and His parable of the lost son in Luke 15 describes a father who runs to meet the one who comes home. The apostles preach the same call, Acts 3:19, and Paul describes the return as the work of God's kindness, Romans 2:4. And when the Spirit is given, the people who could not turn are turned.

The end of the story reverses the chapter. The hunger and thirst of the famines are gone, 'Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst,' Revelation 7:16. The scorching heat is gone. The curse is gone, 'No longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3. And the meeting that Amos announced as a summons has become the meeting for which the redeemed have been made ready, when they see His face. The 'prepare to meet your God' of Amos 4:12 is the question every human being faces, and in the new creation it is answered by a people who have been prepared by a Saviour to meet Him gladly.

quiz.q: What is the point of the repeated refrain, yet you did not return to Me?

options.text: The disasters were merciful warnings meant to turn Israel back, and their refusal to repent is the real tragedy.
options.note: God disciplined in love, aiming at repentance, and Israel would not turn.

options.text: God enjoyed punishing Israel repeatedly.
options.note: The refrain is a lament over refused mercy, not delight in punishment.

options.text: Israel kept suffering hardships that God allowed.
options.note: True, but the point is that each was a call to repent that was rejected.

options.text: God sent hardship hoping Israel would turn back, but they never did.
options.note: Right about the aim of repentance; the deeper note is that impenitence is the tragedy, not the disasters.

quiz.q: Why does God mock Israel with Go to Bethel and transgress?

options.text: Their worship was enthusiastic and frequent but disconnected from justice and obedience, so it was actually sin.
options.note: They loved worship God hated because it masked oppression.

options.text: God wanted them to worship more often.
options.note: The command is sarcastic; their worship was itself rebellion.

options.text: God was rejecting the false shrines at Bethel and Gilgal.
options.note: True, and the sting is that their beloved worship was transgression.

options.text: God preferred worship at Jerusalem instead.
options.note: The issue is heartless, unjust worship, not merely the wrong location.

quiz.q: What does prepare to meet your God mean in this context?

options.text: Because every warning was refused, Israel must now face God Himself as Judge, a terrifying summons that still implies a last call to repent.
options.note: It is a threat of judgment that, until the end, remains a merciful call.

options.text: Israel should get ready for a pleasant encounter with God.
options.note: For the impenitent this is a fearful confrontation, not a pleasant meeting.

options.text: It is a warning that judgment is now unavoidable.
options.note: Right about the judgment; chapter 5's renewed plea shows the door is not yet fully shut.

options.text: It means Israel should prepare more sacrifices.
options.note: God has just rejected their sacrifices; this is about facing Him, not more ritual.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter end with a hymn about God forming mountains and wind?

options.text: The God Israel must meet is the almighty Creator, the LORD of Hosts, whom no one can resist.
options.note: The creation hymn magnifies the God they must face.

options.text: It is an unrelated worship song added at the end.
options.note: It directly crowns the summons to meet God.

options.text: It reminds Israel that God is powerful over nature.
options.note: True, and specifically it underscores the majesty of the God they must prepare to meet.

options.text: It softens the warning with a comforting thought.
options.note: It heightens, not softens, the seriousness of meeting the God of Hosts.

quiz.q: How does Israel's failure to return point us to Christ?

options.text: Even God's disciplines could not make them repent, exposing our need for the Savior who turns the heart and met God's judgment for us.
options.note: The failure of every warning drives the story to Christ.

options.text: It shows people just need to try harder to repent.
options.note: The chapter shows human effort failing; Christ must turn the heart.

options.text: It reminds us God is patient, as Jesus also is.
options.note: True, but the deeper point is our inability to return apart from Christ.

options.text: It proves God had given up on His people entirely.
options.note: God keeps calling; the story moves toward redemption, not abandonment.

questions: God sent hardship as an alarm to turn Israel home. Looking back, where has difficulty been God's way of getting your attention, and how did you respond?
Israel loved worship but not justice. Is there a gap between how much you enjoy religious activity and how much you actually obey God?
The tragedy was not the disasters but the refusal to return. Is there an area where God has been calling you back that you keep resisting?
Everyone must one day prepare to meet God. How does knowing Christ change that meeting from a terror into a homecoming for you?
The One they had to face is the Maker of mountains and wind. How does a bigger vision of God's majesty reshape the way you take His warnings?

translationNotes.note: Cows of Bashan is a deliberately jarring image; Bashan's cattle were proverbially fat and sleek, so the phrase mocks the pampered women of Samaria who feed on the exploitation of the poor.
Cleanness of teeth is a grim idiom for having nothing to eat, empty mouths and empty stomachs, hence the paired phrase lack of bread.
A firebrand snatched from a blaze pictures a partial, painful rescue that should have provoked gratitude and repentance, yet even this did not turn Israel back.
